title: Tiger bread (Dutch crunch)
subtitle: White tin loaf with a crackling rice-paste topping
excerpt: Tiger bread is a soft white loaf topped with a rice flour paste that cracks and blisters as the bread bakes. The paste dries faster than the expanding dough beneath it, forming the distinctive tiger-stripe pattern. Getting the paste consistency right is the key step: it should be thick enough to hold its shape but thin enough to spread without tearing the dough.
sourceNotes: Dutch baking tradition (tijgerbrood), widely documented in public-domain European baking manuals. British Bakeries Association historical records on tin loaf variations.

recipe.freezeNotes: Slice and freeze for up to 2 months.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can prove overnight in the refrigerator; apply the topping paste just before baking.

baking.steamMethod: No steam required; the paste coating creates its own surface

glossaryTerms.definition: The process by which flour proteins bond into elastic strands when mixed with water. Adequate gluten development gives bread structure and allows the dough to trap gas produced by yeast.
A test for gluten development: a small piece of dough is stretched gently between the fingers. If it stretches thin enough to be translucent without tearing, the gluten is sufficiently developed.

content.text: Tiger bread is a soft white tin loaf with a rice flour paste on top that cracks into its characteristic markings as the bread bakes.
You get a pillowy, sandwich-ready crumb beneath a crunchy, lacquered shell that shatters satisfyingly when you slice it.
Watch the paste: too thick and it sits in a solid slab; too thin and it runs off and pools at the tin sides instead of cracking.

attrs.prepNote: warm, about 38 degrees C, for the topping paste

content.text: Method
Making the dough

In a large mixing bowl, combine the strong white flour, caster sugar, and salt. In a separate small bowl or jug, stir the dried yeast into the warm water and leave for 5 minutes until the yeast is frothy. (If using fresh yeast, crumble it directly into the warm water and stir.) Add the sunflower oil to the yeast liquid.

Pour the yeast liquid into the flour mixture. Mix to a shaggy dough, then turn out onto a lightly floured surface and knead for 10 minutes by hand, or for 7 minutes in a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook on medium speed. Proper
gluten development
is key to a loaf that holds its tin shape and has a good, even crumb. The dough is ready when it is smooth, slightly tacky but not sticky, and passes the
windowpane test
: take a small piece of dough and stretch it gently between your fingers. It should stretch thin enough to be semi-translucent without tearing.
First prove

Shape the dough into a ball and place it in a lightly oiled large mixing bowl. Cover with a damp tea towel or cling film and leave in a warm spot (around 24 to 26 degrees C) for 60 minutes, or until roughly doubled in size. An unheated oven with just the light on works well in a cold kitchen.
Making the tiger paste

About 10 minutes before the first prove is complete, make the tiger paste. In a small bowl, stir together the 80 g rice flour, 10 g dried yeast, 10 g caster sugar, 2 g salt, and 5 ml sesame oil. Add the 120 ml of warm water and whisk until you have a smooth paste with no lumps.

The paste should have the consistency of thick double cream: it should coat the back of a spoon and hold a trail, but still be fluid enough to spread easily without pressing. If it is too thick, add warm water a teaspoon at a time. If it is too thin, add rice flour a teaspoon at a time. Leave the paste to sit while you shape the dough. The yeast in the paste activates and creates tiny bubbles that help the cracking effect.
Shaping and the tin

Grease a standard 900 g (2 lb) loaf tin with sunflower oil or line with baking parchment. Knock back the proved dough by pressing it flat with your palms to expel the large gas bubbles. Shape the dough into a log roughly the length of the tin: fold in the two short ends, then roll the dough towards you to form a tight cylinder. Place it seam-side down in the prepared tin.
Second prove

Cover the tin loosely with oiled cling film and leave in a warm spot for 45 to 60 minutes, until the dough has risen about 2 cm above the rim of the tin and feels puffy when gently pressed. Do not let it over-prove: the dough needs room to continue rising in the oven, and an over-proved loaf will have a flat top or may even cave as it bakes.
While the dough has its second prove, preheat your oven to 220 degrees C.
Topping and baking

Give the paste a quick stir. Use a pastry brush or a spoon to apply a generous, even layer of paste over the entire top surface of the proved dough. The layer should be about 3 to 4 mm thick. Do not press down on the dough as you apply it. Leave a small gap at the edges of the tin so the paste does not glue the loaf to the sides.

Place the tin in the middle of the preheated oven. Bake for 28 to 32 minutes. The loaf is done when the topping has cracked into deep amber ridges and the internal temperature reaches 94 degrees C. It should sound hollow when you tap the base. If the paste is colouring faster than the bread is baking, tent loosely with foil.
Remove the loaf from the tin immediately and cool on a rack for at least 30 minutes before slicing. The crust continues to crisp as it cools; slicing too early produces a doughy, compressed crumb.

attrs.problem: The paste did not crack; it set as a smooth, pale shell
attrs.avoid: Avoid applying the paste to a dough that has already fully proved. The paste must go on with some rise still to come in the oven.
attrs.fix: Check that your paste was not too thick or too dry. The yeast in the paste needs to be active (use yeast within its use-by date and mix with warm, not boiling, water). A paste with dead yeast will not create the characteristic crackling surface.

attrs.problem: The paste ran off the sides and pooled at the base of the tin
attrs.avoid: Avoid making the paste too thin. It should be the consistency of thick double cream, not single cream.
attrs.fix: Add rice flour a teaspoon at a time until the paste holds a trail when you lift a spoon and let it fall. Apply it to the dough immediately: a very liquid paste will slide before the heat sets it.

attrs.problem: The loaf is dense with a tight crumb
attrs.avoid: Avoid under-kneading: insufficient gluten development leaves the crumb dense and can prevent the loaf from holding the gas produced during proving.
attrs.fix: Knead for the full 10 minutes by hand, or check the dough passes the windowpane test before resting. Also check your yeast is active: dissolve it in warm water and look for froth within 5 to 10 minutes.

attrs.problem: The top of the loaf is flat or sunken
attrs.avoid: Avoid over-proving the shaped dough. Once the dough is visibly above the rim of the tin and very puffy, bake promptly.
attrs.fix: An over-proved loaf exhausts its gas supply before baking and cannot rise further in the oven. If the dough collapses slightly when you remove the cling film to apply the paste, it has proved too long. Bake immediately at the correct temperature.
